title: Lesson 9: Bar Numbers
subtopics: Creating bar numbers from ordinary numbers
Using bar numbers in sums, subtraction, multiplication, and division
learningGoals: Convert between barred notation and ordinary numbers in both directions.
Use bar numbers to simplify subtraction and to remove awkward large digits.
Recognize when bar form makes a later addition, subtraction, multiplication, or division easier.
coreIdeas: A barred digit is negative, so the number is understood as the next place value minus the barred part.
Splitting after the barred block keeps long bar numbers manageable and visual on the board.
Bar numbers are a working notation that can simplify later arithmetic before the final answer is converted back.

workedExamples.method: This is the plain-number form of two bar one. First show the barred notation, then rewrite it as twenty minus one.
This removes the bar number five bar three three by splitting the number and subtracting the barred block from the next place value.
Subtract each column directly to get a temporary bar-form answer, then convert that bar answer into the ordinary result.
This shows how 287 can be rewritten in bar form as three bar one three, which removes the large digits before later work.

starterPractice: Warm-up: convert two bar one and four bar two into ordinary numbers.
Guided: remove the bar number five bar three three by rewriting it as a subtraction.
Independent: subtract 444 - 286 using bar digits before converting the answer.

onboarding.coachIntro: Raj checks language comfort, current confidence, and session goal before starting Bar Numbers.
onboarding.placementRule: Recommended start level for Lesson 9: familiar. If the learner struggles twice in one step, keep the pace slow and repeat the pattern with a smaller number.

mission.missionPromise: Convert between barred notation and ordinary numbers in both directions.
mission.successCelebration: Celebrate each correct step in Bar Numbers with points, a badge pulse, and a quick coach line before moving on.

microLessonPattern: Coach opens with one short hook and names the pattern.
Coach models one worked move on the board.
Coach reads the exercise question aloud.
Niagh tries before the full answer is shown.
Instant feedback either celebrates or repairs the first mistake.
A quick review prompt decides whether the learner advances or repeats.

rewardLoop.xpUnit: Award 10 to 20 XP per exercise group based on the step position in the lesson path.
rewardLoop.streakRule: Keep the streak visible on every step and protect it with immediate retries instead of long explanations.
rewardLoop.badgeRule: Each exercise group has one badge focus tied to the subtopic being learned.
rewardLoop.celebrationStyle: Short praise, points pulse, and progress-bar movement after every correct response.

reviewLoop.trigger: If the learner answers incorrectly, hesitates, or shows low confidence, reopen the same pattern with one smaller follow-up.
reviewLoop.practiceStyle: Use the micro-practice line as the first repair loop before advancing.
reviewLoop.masteryRule: Advance only after the learner can answer the checkpoint and complete one try in the same subtopic.
reviewLoop.revisitRule: Weak steps should return in the next session as review cards before new content.

uiDirectives.noScrollGoal: The learner should see mission progress, the current question, and the main action buttons without long vertical scrolling.

sessionFlow.missionStepTitle: Exercise A: Removing a single barred digit
sessionFlow.coachHook: A bar digit means that digit is negative, so two bar one means twenty minus one and therefore nineteen.
sessionFlow.boardDemo: Write 21 with a bar over the 1, say 'two bar one', then rewrite it as 20 - 1 = 19.
sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Why does two bar one stand for nineteen?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Niagh, try this one. Say your first step, then your answer.
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: Why does two bar one stand for nineteen?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct. Removing a single barred digit is now stronger and ready for the next step.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: The barred digit is subtracted, not added.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Convert three bar one and four bar two into ordinary numbers.

sessionFlow.missionStepTitle: Exercise B: Splitting after the bar
sessionFlow.coachHook: When the bar appears inside a longer number, split immediately after the barred block and convert each part calmly.
sessionFlow.boardDemo: Write five one bar three, split it as 51 / bar3, then convert the first part before reattaching the last digit block.
sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Why do we split after the barred block when removing a bar number inside a longer number?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Niagh, try this one. Say your first step, then your answer.
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: Why do we split after the barred block when removing a bar number inside a longer number?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct. Splitting after the bar is now stronger and ready for the next step.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Do not try to convert the whole number at once.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Convert five one bar three two and three bar two one five by splitting after the barred part.

sessionFlow.missionStepTitle: Exercise C: Several barred digits together
sessionFlow.coachHook: When several barred digits come together, think of one block being taken away from the next place value and use complements on the barred part.
sessionFlow.boardDemo: Show seven bar one four as 700 - 14 and five zero bar three as 500 - 3, then connect this to Lesson 5 complements.
sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: How does seven bar one four turn into six hundred eighty-six?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Niagh, try this one. Say your first step, then your answer.
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: How does seven bar one four turn into six hundred eighty-six?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct. Several barred digits together is now stronger and ready for the next step.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Treat the barred tail as one amount being subtracted.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Convert seven bar zero two and four bar two three one into ordinary numbers.

sessionFlow.missionStepTitle: Exercise D: Subtraction by allowing barred digits
sessionFlow.coachHook: In subtraction, each column can be subtracted directly, and any negative column is written as a barred digit before the answer is converted.
sessionFlow.boardDemo: Set up 444 - 286 vertically, subtract each column straight down, write 2 bar4 bar2, and then convert it to 158.
sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Why does direct column subtraction still work after we rewrite negative columns as barred digits?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Niagh, try this one. Say your first step, then your answer.
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: Why does direct column subtraction still work after we rewrite negative columns as barred digits?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct. Subtraction by allowing barred digits is now stronger and ready for the next step.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: We subtract each column as it stands.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Subtract 6767 - 1908 by writing every column result first and converting only at the end.

sessionFlow.subtopic: Creating bar numbers from ordinary numbers
sessionFlow.missionStepTitle: Exercise E: Creating bar numbers from ordinary numbers
sessionFlow.coachHook: To create a bar number, push the earlier place value up by one and turn the high tail into its complement.
sessionFlow.boardDemo: Write 79, 239, and 7689; then rewrite them as 8 bar1, 24 bar1, and 769 bar1 using the board one place at a time.
sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Why does seventy-nine become eight bar one?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Niagh, try this one. Say your first step, then your answer.
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: Why does seventy-nine become eight bar one?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct. Creating bar numbers from ordinary numbers is now stronger and ready for the next step.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Put fifty-eight, eighty-eight, and six hundred nine into bar form.

sessionFlow.missionStepTitle: Exercise F: Using bar numbers in sums, subtraction, multiplication, and division
sessionFlow.coachHook: Once a number is in a convenient bar form, we can add, subtract, multiply, or divide with smaller digits and convert back only at the end.
sessionFlow.boardDemo: Work through 29 + 48, 623 - 188, 29 x 3, and 87 / 3 by converting one number into bar form before the operation.
sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: When is it worth converting to bar form before doing the main operation?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Niagh, try this one. Say your first step, then your answer.
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: When is it worth converting to bar form before doing the main operation?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct. Using bar numbers in sums, subtraction, multiplication, and division is now stronger and ready for the next step.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Choose the conversion only when it makes the digits friendlier.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Use bar form to simplify 29 + 48 and 29 x 3, then explain why the digits became easier.

screenplay.teacherLine: A bar number is a compact way to say a number is just below the next place value.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 21 with a bar over the 1 and read it aloud as two bar one.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does two bar one stand for nineteen?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The barred digit is subtracted, not added.

screenplay.teacherLine: Two bar one means twenty minus one, so it equals nineteen.
screenplay.boardAction: Rewrite it as 20 - 1 = 19 under the bar notation.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does two bar one stand for nineteen?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The place value stays twenty, and the barred digit comes off it.

screenplay.teacherLine: The same pattern gives three bar one as twenty-nine and four bar two as thirty-eight.
screenplay.boardAction: Reveal 30 - 1 = 29 and 40 - 2 = 38 one line at a time.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does two bar one stand for nineteen?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Increase the place value, then subtract the barred digit.

screenplay.teacherLine: Now convert six bar one without jumping straight to the answer.
screenplay.boardAction: Show 60 - 1 = __ with the bar notation still visible.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does two bar one stand for nineteen?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Replace the bar form by subtraction first.

screenplay.teacherLine: Checkpoint: say the rule for a single barred digit in one sentence.
screenplay.boardAction: Box the phrase place value minus barred digit.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does two bar one stand for nineteen?
screenplay.expectedStudentResponse: Read the place value, then subtract the barred digit.
screenplay.fallbackHint: That sentence is the whole conversion rule.

screenplay.teacherLine: A bar in the middle of a number is easier when we break the number into pieces.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 51 with a bar over the 3 and draw a split mark after the barred digit.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why do we split after the barred block when removing a bar number inside a longer number?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Do not try to convert the whole number at once.

screenplay.teacherLine: Five one bar three is treated as 51 slash bar3, so the front part changes first.
screenplay.boardAction: Show 51 -> 49 and keep the barred 3 aside.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why do we split after the barred block when removing a bar number inside a longer number?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Only the part ending at the barred digit changes.

screenplay.teacherLine: Now reattach the last block, so five one bar three becomes four hundred ninety-three.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 49 followed by 3 to make 493.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why do we split after the barred block when removing a bar number inside a longer number?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Split, convert, reattach.

screenplay.teacherLine: Use the same split method on five bar three three, which means five hundred minus thirty-three.
screenplay.boardAction: Show 500 - 33 = __ beside the bar form.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why do we split after the barred block when removing a bar number inside a longer number?
screenplay.fallbackHint: This is the same idea as all from 9 and the last from 10.

screenplay.teacherLine: Checkpoint: what are the three board moves for a bar number inside a longer number?
screenplay.boardAction: Leave split, convert, reattach as three short labels.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why do we split after the barred block when removing a bar number inside a longer number?
screenplay.expectedStudentResponse: Split after the bar, convert the front, then reattach the rest.
screenplay.fallbackHint: That order prevents mistakes.

screenplay.teacherLine: A block of barred digits behaves like one subtraction from the next place value.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 714 with bars over 1 and 4, then rewrite it as 700 - 14.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How does seven bar one four turn into six hundred eighty-six?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Treat the barred tail as one amount being subtracted.

screenplay.teacherLine: Seven hundred minus fourteen is six hundred eighty-six, so the bar form hides a simple subtraction.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 700 - 14 = 686 directly below.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How does seven bar one four turn into six hundred eighty-six?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The plain-number form is easier to read once converted.

screenplay.teacherLine: Five zero bar three is five hundred minus three, which is four hundred ninety-seven.
screenplay.boardAction: Reveal 500 - 3 = 497 and point out the reduced hundred.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How does seven bar one four turn into six hundred eighty-six?
screenplay.fallbackHint: A zero can be part of the barred block too.

screenplay.teacherLine: Now convert seven bar zero two by rewriting it first.
screenplay.boardAction: Show 700 - 2 = __ with the bar number above it.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How does seven bar one four turn into six hundred eighty-six?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The barred 02 means subtract two from seven hundred.

screenplay.teacherLine: Checkpoint: why do complements help when the barred tail has more than one digit?
screenplay.boardAction: Leave 33 -> 67 and 14 -> 86 on the side of the board.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How does seven bar one four turn into six hundred eighty-six?
screenplay.expectedStudentResponse: They show what remains after one place value is reduced.
screenplay.fallbackHint: Lesson 5 complements and bar numbers fit together.

screenplay.teacherLine: Bar numbers give a new way to subtract without borrowing first.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 444 over 286 and draw the subtraction line.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does direct column subtraction still work after we rewrite negative columns as barred digits?
screenplay.fallbackHint: We subtract each column as it stands.

screenplay.teacherLine: Four minus two is two, four minus eight is negative four, and four minus six is negative two.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 2, then bar4, then bar2 under the columns.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does direct column subtraction still work after we rewrite negative columns as barred digits?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Negative column answers are allowed for the moment.

screenplay.teacherLine: Two bar four bar two converts to one hundred fifty-eight.
screenplay.boardAction: Rewrite 2 bar4 bar2 as 158 in a second line.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does direct column subtraction still work after we rewrite negative columns as barred digits?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The temporary barred answer is only an intermediate form.

screenplay.teacherLine: Now try 6767 minus 1908 by direct column subtraction.
screenplay.boardAction: Show the columns with blanks for 6-1, 7-9, 6-0, and 7-8.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does direct column subtraction still work after we rewrite negative columns as barred digits?
screenplay.expectedStudentResponse: Five bar two six bar one, then 4859.
screenplay.fallbackHint: First write the column results, then convert the bar number.

screenplay.teacherLine: Checkpoint: when do we convert the bar answer back to an ordinary number?
screenplay.boardAction: Underline the final bar-form line before the ordinary answer.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does direct column subtraction still work after we rewrite negative columns as barred digits?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Do not mix borrowing with the bar method.

screenplay.subtopic: Creating bar numbers from ordinary numbers
screenplay.teacherLine: Bar form is useful because it removes large digits like seven, eight, and nine.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 79 and circle the 9 as a large digit.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does seventy-nine become eight bar one?
screenplay.fallbackHint: We want smaller trailing digits.

screenplay.subtopic: Creating bar numbers from ordinary numbers
screenplay.teacherLine: Seventy-nine is one less than eighty, so it becomes eight bar one.
screenplay.boardAction: Rewrite 79 as 80 - 1 and then as 8 with a barred 1.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does seventy-nine become eight bar one?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Move up one place value, then bar the complement.

screenplay.subtopic: Creating bar numbers from ordinary numbers
screenplay.teacherLine: Two hundred thirty-nine becomes two hundred forty minus one, so it is two four bar one.
screenplay.boardAction: Show 240 - 1 = 239 next to the bar form.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does seventy-nine become eight bar one?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The same push-up rule works inside longer numbers.

screenplay.subtopic: Creating bar numbers from ordinary numbers
screenplay.teacherLine: Now turn seven thousand six hundred eighty-nine into bar form by handling the last two digits together.
screenplay.boardAction: Show 7700 - 11 = __ and leave the bar form blank.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does seventy-nine become eight bar one?
screenplay.expectedStudentResponse: Seven six nine bar one or seven seven bar one one, depending on the chosen grouping.
screenplay.fallbackHint: Push the front up and complement the tail.

screenplay.subtopic: Creating bar numbers from ordinary numbers
screenplay.teacherLine: Checkpoint: what problem do bar numbers solve when digits are too large?
screenplay.boardAction: Leave a side note saying avoid large digits 6, 7, 8, 9.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does seventy-nine become eight bar one?
screenplay.expectedStudentResponse: They replace large digits with smaller barred complements.
screenplay.fallbackHint: That is why later calculations become easier.

screenplay.subtopic: Using bar numbers in sums, subtraction, multiplication, and division
screenplay.teacherLine: Bar numbers are not a topic by themselves only; they are a working tool inside other operations.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 29 + 48 and 29 x 3 side by side.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: When is it worth converting to bar form before doing the main operation?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Choose the conversion only when it makes the digits friendlier.

screenplay.subtopic: Using bar numbers in sums, subtraction, multiplication, and division
screenplay.teacherLine: Twenty-nine can become three bar one, and forty-eight can become five bar two, so 29 + 48 stays balanced at 77.
screenplay.boardAction: Show 31 + 48 and 29 + 52 leading to 77.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: When is it worth converting to bar form before doing the main operation?
screenplay.fallbackHint: A bar conversion changes the look, not the value.

screenplay.subtopic: Using bar numbers in sums, subtraction, multiplication, and division
screenplay.teacherLine: For multiplication, 29 x 3 becomes 31 x 3 = 93, which converts to 87.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 31 x 3 = 93, then convert 93 to 87.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: When is it worth converting to bar form before doing the main operation?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The barred form may make the multiplication easier.

screenplay.subtopic: Using bar numbers in sums, subtraction, multiplication, and division
screenplay.teacherLine: Use the same idea in subtraction with 623 - 188 becoming 623 - 212.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 212 under 623 and ask for the answer.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: When is it worth converting to bar form before doing the main operation?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The bar form of 188 makes the subtraction cleaner.

screenplay.subtopic: Using bar numbers in sums, subtraction, multiplication, and division
screenplay.teacherLine: Final checkpoint: name one sign that bar form will help before you start a question.
screenplay.boardAction: Leave four boxes labelled add, subtract, multiply, divide.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: When is it worth converting to bar form before doing the main operation?
screenplay.expectedStudentResponse: When there are large awkward digits that can be replaced by smaller complements.
screenplay.fallbackHint: Bar numbers are a choice, not a compulsory step.

teachingFlowStages.intent: Introduce barred digits as a visual way to show a number just below the next place value.
Explain single barred digits, split-bar numbers, and grouped barred tails with visible board rewrites.
Demonstrate conversions and subtraction with direct column work before converting back.
Have the learner say the rewrite first, then the final ordinary-number answer.
Mix conversion, subtraction, and large-digit removal tasks in increasing difficulty.
Verify that each bar form and ordinary form really represent the same value.
Require the learner to choose when bar form is worth using inside a larger problem.
